entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nomus (fl. c. 443–450 CE) was a powerful Eastern Roman statesman and diplomat who rose to the highest offices of the imperial court during the tumultuous mid-5th century, serving under emperors Theodosius II and Marcian. His career was defined by his crucial role in managing the volatile relationship between the Eastern Roman Empire and the burgeoning Huns under Attila, a period that profoundly shaped the geopolitical landscape of late antiquity. As *magister officiorum* and later *patricius*, Nomus wielded immense influence over imperial administration and foreign policy, navigating the complex threats posed by barbarian incursions and internal political machinations.

Nomus's most significant contributions stemmed from his diplomatic missions to Attila's court. In 443 CE, following devastating Hunnic raids that pushed to the walls of Constantinople, he was instrumental in negotiating a new, significantly more onerous peace treaty, likely involving an increased annual tribute of 700 pounds of gold and the return of Roman fugitives. His appointment as *magister officiorum* in 443 further solidified his control over the imperial secretariat and intelligence services. In 449 CE, he played a central, albeit controversial, role in the embassy to Attila led by Maximin, which famously included the historian Priscus of Panium, whose detailed account provides much of our knowledge of Nomus's activities. This mission, ostensibly to settle disputes, was covertly entangled with a Byzantine assassination plot against Attila, orchestrated by the eunuch Chrysaphius and Vigilas, a plan that ultimately failed but revealed the desperation of Constantinople.

The magister officiorum was one of the most powerful positions in the late Roman bureaucracy — controlling the imperial chancery, the scholae palatinae (palace guards), the cursus publicus (imperial postal system), and the frontier fortifications. Nomus was thus a man of extraordinary administrative influence in one of the most turbulent decades of the late Western and Eastern Roman empires.

Nomus's career spans the period of Attila the Hun's greatest threat to the Roman world: the massive Hunnic invasions of the Balkans (441–443 CE, 447–449 CE) that devastated Eastern Roman territory, forced huge tribute payments, and brought Roman ambassadors — including the historian Priscus, whose account of his visit to Attila's court is one of the most remarkable documents of late antiquity — to negotiate at the Hunnic court. Nomus himself was involved in the diplomatic management of the Hunnic crisis — he was part of the extensive Byzantine diplomatic apparatus that sought to manage Attila through tribute, gifts, and negotiation while the Eastern Empire lacked the military capacity to defeat him in the field.

Nomus also played a role in religious politics: the reign of Theodosius II was marked by the great Christological controversies of the Nestorian dispute and the Council of Ephesus (431 CE), and the court's religious policies significantly shaped his career context. historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nomus played a critical role in Eastern Roman diplomacy with Attila the Hun, directly contributing to the temporary preservation of Constantinople's stability and the Eastern Empire's survival through its most perilous early encounters with the Huns. His actions bought valuable time, allowing the East to consolidate power while the West crumbled.
